title: Four readings in one place
prompt:
A patient's systolic pressure was taken four times over a shift: 118,
142, 131 and 156.

R's function for putting several values together is `c()`, short for
*combine*. Use it to store all four in one variable called `sbp`.
hint: The function name goes directly before the opening bracket.

solution.why:
`c()` combines values into a *vector* — one name holding several
values in order. Almost everything you do with data in R is done to
vectors.

checks.on_fail: `sbp` should hold all four readings, in the order they were taken.

misconceptions.feedback:
`list()` does exist and does hold several things, but it's a
different, looser container — you'll meet it in module 10. For
values that are all the same kind, you want `c()`.

title: Which one is second?
prompt:
Square brackets pick a value out of a vector by its position.

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
sbp[2]
```

What does the second line return?
hint: Count the way you'd count anything else.

options.feedback:
Right. R counts from 1, the way people do: the first value is
`sbp[1]`, the second is `sbp[2]`. That sounds too obvious to
mention, but almost every other programming language counts from 0 —
so if you ever read Python, `readings[2]` there means the *third*
value.

That's what you'd get if R counted from 0, which Python and most
other languages do. R counts from 1, so position 2 is the second
value. Worth remembering: this is the single most common source of
confusion when people move between the two.

The number inside the brackets picks one position. To get all four
you'd type `sbp` on its own, instead of `sbp[2]`.

title: Arithmetic on the whole thing
prompt:
The cuff was reading 10 mmHg higher than the patient's true pressure all
shift. What does the last line return?

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
sbp - 10
```
hint: `sbp` holds four numbers. Nothing in this line picks just one of them.

options.feedback:
Yes. Arithmetic on a vector happens to every value at once. You
didn't have to say "for each reading, subtract 10" — R did it to
all four without being asked.

R applies it to every value, not only the first. There's no need to
say which ones; the whole vector is the default.

options.text: An error — you can't subtract a number from a vector
options.feedback:
You can, and it's one of the most useful things about R. The 10 is
taken from each value in turn.

title: Did that change anything?
prompt:
You run these lines, in this order.

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
sbp - 10
sbp
```

What does the last line print?

options.feedback:
Right. `sbp - 10` works out four corrected values and hands them
back, but nothing catches them — there's no arrow, so nothing is
stored. `sbp` is exactly what it was. To keep the correction you'd
write `sbp <- sbp - 10`, which replaces the old readings, silently,
the way reassignment always does.

The subtraction happened, but its result was never stored. A
calculation returns a value; only `<-` stores one. Without an arrow,
`sbp` is untouched.

options.text: An error, because `sbp` was used up by the first line
options.feedback:
Using a variable doesn't consume it. You can read `sbp` as many
times as you like and it stays the same until something is assigned
to it.

title: Asking every reading a question
hint:
In module 3, `118 > 140` gave you one answer. How many values are in
`sbp`?

options.feedback:
Yes — one answer per reading. The comparison was asked of every
value, just like the subtraction was. This is what module 3
promised: a thousand blood pressures and one question gives you a
thousand TRUEs and FALSEs — and you can use that list to pick out
the values you care about.

options.text: `TRUE` — because some of them are over 140
options.feedback:
R doesn't summarise the answer for you. It asks the question of each
value separately and gives you all four answers back.

That's where this is heading, but it's one step further. A
comparison gives you TRUE or FALSE for each value. Turning those into
the values themselves is the last exercise in this module.

title: How many were high?
prompt:
`sbp > 140` gives you `FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE`. You want to know how many
readings were over 140.

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
______(sbp > 140)
```

Which function goes in the blank?
hint: Remember what `TRUE + TRUE` gave you in module 3.

options.feedback:
Right. `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, so adding up the answers
gives you 2 — the number that were over 140. It looked like a
curiosity in module 3; this is what it's for.

`length()` gives you 4 — the number of answers, one per reading. It
counts how many values there are, not how many of them are TRUE.

`mean()` gives you 0.5. Not the count, but a genuinely useful answer
to a different question: what *fraction* of readings were over 140.
Half of them.

`max()` gives you 1, which tells you that *at least one* reading was
over 140. It can't tell you how many.

title: One value in quotes
prompt:
One reading was typed in with quotes around it. What does the last line
return?

```r
readings <- c(118, "142", 131)
class(readings)
```
hint: A vector can only hold one type of value. Something has to give.

options.feedback:
Yes. A vector holds one type only, so when one value is text R turns
*all* of them into text to make them match. `118` is now `"118"`.

This is exactly how real data arrives, whether it's a lab export or
a large research database. One entry says `"<0.5"` or `"hemolysed"`
or `"not done"`, and the whole column comes in as text. Nothing
warns you at the time. It only shows up later, when arithmetic or
other functions don't give you what you expect — and it keeps
happening until the mismatch is dealt with.

options.text: `"numeric"`, because most of them are numbers
options.feedback:
R doesn't take a majority vote. One text value is enough to make the
whole vector text, because text can hold a number but a number
can't hold text.

That would make sense if each value kept its own type. It can't: a
vector is one type throughout, so R converts them all to the type
that can hold everything.

title: Why is the mean NA?
prompt:
You were handed this to get the average systolic. Press **Run it** to see
what happens.

The warning comes from `mean()` — but `mean()` isn't what's wrong. Click
the part of the code that *caused* the problem.
hint:
The help page for `mean()` says it needs a numeric or logical vector —
the **Functions** panel says the same. What kind of vector is `sbp`?

options.feedback:
This one is a plain number. It's the value two places along that's
different.

Right. One quoted value turned the whole vector into text, and
`mean()` only works on numbers — its help page says so, and so does
the Functions panel. This is why
types matter at all: most functions only accept certain kinds of
value, and when they're handed the wrong kind, they either stop or
quietly give you something useless.

Notice how this one failed: not an error that stopped everything, but
a warning and an `NA` that's easy to scroll past. Nobody checks
`class()` before they start — the skill is what you just did, working
backwards from a strange result to what caused it. When a function
gives you something odd, `class()` is a good first question to ask.

This is where the warning comes from, but `mean()` is doing exactly
its job. It was handed four pieces of text instead of four numbers,
and its warning says so. The problem was made one line earlier.

title: Rescue the numbers
prompt:
`sbp` is still text, so `mean(sbp)` still gives `NA`. And you can't always
just delete the quotes — often the data came from somewhere else.

First, a new idea. You can put one function call *inside* another. R runs
the inside one first, then hands its result to the outside one:

```r
round(sqrt(2), 1)
```

`sqrt(2)` runs first and gives about 1.414. Then `round()` gets that and
gives 1.4.

Now the function you need: **`as.numeric()` converts text into
numbers.** Put it inside `mean()` to get the average of `sbp`.
hint: Convert first, then average. `as.numeric(sbp)` goes where the blank is.

solution.why:
`as.numeric(sbp)` returns a vector of four numbers, and that vector is
handed straight to `mean()`. A call inside a call runs from the inside
out. The original `sbp` is still text afterwards — nothing was stored.

checks.on_fail:
Not 136.75 yet. The values need converting to numbers before
they're averaged.

misconceptions.feedback:
The output of `mean()` is still `NA`, so it's still being handed
text. Put `as.numeric(sbp)` inside the brackets of `mean()`, so the
conversion happens first.

`as.character()` converts the other way — into text, which is the
problem you already have. You want `as.numeric()`.

title: Highest first
prompt:
`sort()` puts values in order. By default it goes lowest first, which
isn't what you want — you want the highest reading at the top.

Its usage line — from the help page, and in the **Functions** panel —
is:

```r
sort(x, decreasing = FALSE, ...)
```
hint: You've overridden a default before, in `log(100, base = 10)`.

solution.why:
The default is written right there in the usage line. `TRUE` here is
the same logical value from module 3 — arguments can take TRUE and
FALSE as settings, and many do.

checks.on_fail:
Not highest-first yet. Check the name of the argument in the usage
line, and what it needs to be set to.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's still lowest-first, which is the default. The argument that
controls it is `decreasing`, and it's currently `FALSE`.

title: Just the high ones
prompt: Using square brackets, get the actual readings that were over 140.
hint:
You already know how to ask which readings are over 140. Put that
question inside the brackets.

solution.why:
`sbp > 140` gives `FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE`, and the brackets keep the
values lined up with each TRUE. That's filtering. When you later
filter a table of a thousand patients, this is what's happening
underneath.

checks.on_fail:
Not the two high readings yet. The question you're asking is:
*which of these readings are over 140?* Write that question in R,
and put it inside the brackets.

misconceptions.feedback:
Check the brackets. There are two pairs here — the square ones
around the question, and the question itself — and one hasn't been
closed.

That's the question's answer, not the readings. Put it *inside* the
brackets after `sbp` so R keeps only the matching values.

That counts how many were high — the previous exercise. Here you
want the readings themselves.
